- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33), model underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is falling.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots in next period; cap forecast at 1–2% below true peak.
- If model forecast is significantly below true outcome (e.g., >5% gap), and sentiment is neutral or positive, consider mean reversion bias — adjust forecast upward by 1–3%.
- If model consistently forecasts higher than true outcome over 3–5 days, check for lag: true price often peaks 1–2 days after model’s peak; shift forecast horizon backward by 1–2 days.
- In high-sentiment volatility periods (e.g., sentiment >0.75 for 3+ days), model tends to overreact; dampen forecast slope or reduce magnitude of expected moves.
- If true outcome shows strong upward trend (e.g., >10% over 3 days) and model underperforms, consider sentiment-driven momentum — increase forecast by 1–2% per day if sentiment >0.67.
- If model forecast is below true outcome by >5% for 3+ consecutive days, consider sentiment reversal — if sentiment drops below 0.33, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overcorrection.
